Ellipse In Arbelos

GeometryCircles
Game: This is a picture, not a game: two touching circles hold a crescent with a chain of circles inside it.
How to play: Drag the point C along the straight line, or focus it and use the arrow keys. Change the sliders to add circles or move the chain, and watch where the centres go.
Look for the math

Move C and the two circles change size. The blue circles still fit in the gap, and every centre lands on the same dashed ellipse. What fixes that curve?

Two distances that add up

Let the small circle have radius a1 and the big one radius a2, with a2 > a1. A gap circle of radius r touches the small circle from outside and the big circle from inside. Its centre is therefore a1 + r from the small centre and a2 − r from the big centre. Adding gives the constant

(a1 + r) + (a2 − r) = a1 + a2

The set of points whose distances from two fixed points add to a constant is an ellipse. Those two fixed points are the centres of the given circles: the ellipse's foci.

The two widths of the ellipse

The foci sit a2 − a1 apart, and the constant sum is a1 + a2, so the long semiaxis is the arithmetic mean (a1 + a2)/2. At the top of the ellipse the three centres make an isosceles triangle. Pythagoras gives

h² = ((a1 + a2)/2)² − ((a2 − a1)/2)² = a1 a2

So the short semiaxis is the geometric mean √(a1 a2). The article's printed formula has the root; a plain-text copy that drops it is just a transcription loss. The logic test checks both widths over 200 positions of C.

The chain of touching circles

Write τ = a1 a2 + s²(a2 − a1)². Then the circle with radius r = a1 a2 (a2 − a1)/τ and centre (a1 a2 (a1 + a2)/τ, 2 s r) fits the gap for any real s, and y = 2 s r. Each circle in this chain touches A1, A2 and its neighbour. The article proves this by inversion: the chain becomes a row of equal circles between two parallel lines. The test checks the distances directly for negative, fractional and large values of s. It also confirms the article's extras: the contact chord passes through (2 a1 a2/(a1 + a2), 0), that point makes a harmonic set with 0, a1 and a2, and when the small diameter is two thirds of the big one, r at s = 1 is one seventh of the big diameter.

About the original

The applet had a number spinner from 1 to 20 circles and a scrollbar from −300 to 300, read as a shift from −15 to 15; both are kept here. It picked the starting C at random near the middle of AB. This page starts it exactly in the middle, and keeps C a few pixels off the ends so the circles do not collapse. Its own "about" text was a leftover from a polygon applet and is not reproduced. Everything else, including the order of the chain s = T, T+1, T−1, T+2, …, follows the bytecode. The page still embeds the Java applet, so no archive was needed.

Set the chain shift to 0, then move C: the first circle becomes the largest gap circle, still with its centre on the dashed ellipse.
